subtitle: An argument that Telnet's Go-Ahead signal is clumsy, unreliable and should be dropped or made optional.

tldr.problem: The Telnet specification required hosts to implement a Go-Ahead (GA) command for passing control between computer and terminal.
tldr.mechanism: The author argues GA is unappealing, will not work without unwarranted assumptions about other hosts, and cannot be implemented correctly by most hosts, with a deadlock example.
tldr.outcome: He advocates removing GA entirely, or making it a negotiated option whose default state is suppressed.

today: This is a position paper whose status is listed as Unknown in the unit metadata, and no later RFC is recorded as replacing it. It asks for GA to be removed or made a negotiated option that is suppressed by default.

sections.title: The Objection to Go-Ahead
sections.content:
E. Taft of PARC-MAXC objects to the requirement that hosts implement the Telnet Go-Ahead (GA) command. His three lines of attack are that GA is esthetically unappealing, that as specified it will not generally serve its purpose, and that most hosts cannot implement it correctly in all cases. He cites PDP-10 systems 10/50 and Tenex.

He wants GA either completely removed or turned into a negotiated option whose default state is that it is suppressed.
sections.eli5: One person says a rule in the networking handbook is awkward, often does not work, and is hard to follow. He wants it gone or switched off by default.

sections.title: Half-Duplex and Reverse Break
sections.content:
Half-duplex means transmission goes in only one direction at a time, and the receiver may not transmit until the sender has explicitly given up control (turned the line around). The author notes this is different from the common but incorrect use of half-duplex and full-duplex to mean local and remote echoing.

A reverse break lets a computer on a half-duplex path regain the line for more typeout. It is the complement of the break or attention mechanism by which a user gains control of the line.
sections.eli5: Half-duplex is like a walkie-talkie: one side talks while the other waits for them to say they are done.

sections.title: Why GA Is Unappealing and Won't Work
sections.content:
The Telnet specification assumes the normal mode is half-duplex, line-at-a-time. The author says the trend is toward interactive full-duplex systems, and that GA mostly serves IBM 2741 terminals via TIPs with reverse break. He also notes that most parties would immediately negotiate to suppress GA, so the default should be the one most hosts accept.

His deadlock example: a user's line is split by the NCP into two messages. The server process reads the first part, blocks, and the server Telnet sends GA. The user's keyboard unlocks while the rest of the output is blocked, until the user manually gives control back. Sending GA only after an end-of-line is a poor fix, because the server cannot know the user host's end-of-line.
sections.eli5: If the "your turn" signal arrives too early, both sides get stuck waiting for the other, like two people each saying "after you" at a door.

sections.title: Implementation Problems
sections.content:
For full-duplex hosts the problems are worse. Subsystems such as the user Telnet, FTP and RJE programs never block for input but poll for it, so GA would never be sent. A process and terminal are not always one-to-one, as in Tenex where one fork may wait for input while another writes output.

Inter-terminal links such as the Tenex LINK facility break the model, and broadcast messages (SEND ALL in 10/50, NOTIFY in Tenex) would be blocked by a half-duplex terminal left in the typein state by an earlier GA.
sections.eli5: Many computers do several jobs at once, so a simple "your turn" flag cannot tell which job is waiting for you.
